annotationRationale: The primary method gives an explicit bijection between eligible arrays and pairs of row and column permutations. The alternative counts the reduced arrays directly using the multiplication principle.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is correct; no repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: Independent counting gives 576, choice D. The example has row sums 3,2,4,1 and column sums 2,4,3,1, so it satisfies the stem. No statement or choice contradiction is present.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: Both Random Math routes are retained: sorting and permuting the unique array, and directly counting the reduced array. LIVE's 24·4·6 construction is an equivalent staged count and needs no additional method. No shared-bank methods were supplied.
review.annotationCheck: Bijective counting is an appropriate assessed concept for the primary route. Permutations and the multiplication principle are suitable supports; the direct-count alternative appropriately uses the multiplication principle alone.
review.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is correct; no repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: Sorting uniquely orders the distinct row and column sums. Removing the forced all-one boundaries, then all-zero boundaries, determines the displayed array uniquely. Distinct sums recover both permutations, so all and only the valid arrays are counted once: \((4!)^2=576\).
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Accurately credits Random Math's permutation route as nonofficial, source-informed work. The specialized uniqueness proof and explanation of nonduplication are original expansions of that argument.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The opening explains why sorting helps, and each forced reduction is reconstructible. The converse and nonduplication argument complete the counting proof.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: All three IDs match the derivation: an explicit invertible correspondence, factorial permutation counts, and multiplication of the two counts.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The all-one row and column have 16 possible positions. The reduced array has three ones: choose its two-one row in 3 ways, its zero in 3 ways, and the last one in 2 other rows and 2 occupied columns. These recoverable choices give \(16\cdot3\cdot3\cdot2\cdot2=576\).

methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The formerly compressed factor of 4 is fully explained. The forbidden empty-column placement and recovery of every choice establish completeness without overcounting.
